situation.note: my son has been in germany nine years. his wife is german, lovely girl. they will not come back I know this. I taught 2000 children and I cannot teach my own heart to stop waiting for him

understanding.bridge: The waiting you cannot stop is what the texts call grief: love with nowhere to go, and the heart aching because the bond was real.
understanding.week_thesis: By the end of the week the waiting has a name, and the love that cannot land is given a place to rest.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the restlessness and the waiting, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the waiting is not a failure. It is love with nowhere to go.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in you cannot be taken by distance.
week_beats.act: You try giving the love a form it can hold, and sitting with the ache without fighting it.
week_beats.story: A father who waited for a son he thought lost shows you how to let the waiting become something you can carry.

understanding.core_struggle: A retired teacher who shaped thousands of students cannot teach his own heart to stop waiting for his son abroad.
understanding.mirror: You taught two thousand children, and the one you cannot teach is your own heart.
understanding.insight: You have taught two thousand children. The one you cannot teach is your own heart, and the reason is that the bond is still real.

queries.hook: The restless waiting for a son who is not coming back, and the ache of a love that has no place to land.
queries.diagnose: Grief is love with nowhere to go; the heart aches because the bond was real, and nothing can be done to make the waiting stop.
queries.steady: What is real in us cannot be taken by distance, and the bond that made you a father is not undone by years.
queries.act: Let the waiting be what it is, and give the love a form it can hold: write him a letter you do not send, or sit with the ache without fighting it.
queries.story: A father who waited for a son he thought lost, and found that the waiting itself was the last lesson he had to teach.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

matched.label: I can't focus, my mind is restless

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands in the field of with a mind that will not settle. He tells Krishna that his thoughts are turbulent and stubborn, like the wind. He cannot pin them down. Krishna agrees, and says that the mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go can train it over time.
verse.for_you: You have taught thousands of minds to settle, but your own will not stop waiting. The restlessness is real. Let the mind be stormy for a while. Practice is not about forcing it still, but about letting go, one moment at a time. You can let the wind blow.
verse.try_today: Sit with the mind without forcing it to settle.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own field, watching a mind that will not settle.
asks: How do I practice letting go of the waiting?
What does letting go look like for me today?

verse.speaker: Kausalya
verse.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
verse.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
verse.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
verse.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
verse.why: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
verse.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.

prasang.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

verse.for_you: What is real in you cannot be taken or lost; only what changes can be taken, and you are more than what changes.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
verse.sanskrit: न ह्यहानि निवर्तन्ते न मासा न पुनः समाः / जातानां सर्वभूतानां न पुनर्वै समागमः
verse.line: Days don't come back, nor months, nor years. Be here for the ones in front of you.
verse.translation: Days do not come back, nor months, nor years. And beings, once parted, do not meet again in the same way.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the sage Ashma how to bear the loss of family and wealth. Ashma answers that pain comes from what we lost and from what we did not want. Meetings end, and days do not come back. Once beings part, they do not meet again in the same way. The heart must grieve, then steady itself with the people still in front of you.
verse.for_you: Do what you can today, take refuge in what does not change, and meet each moment with courage instead of rehearsing the worst.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing your children or parents do today that you can hold onto.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own hall, waiting for a door that will not open today.
asks: How do I stop the waiting from wearing down my days?
Can the people still here truly steady me?
How do I grieve and still be here?

verse.speaker: Sita
verse.setting: Alone in captivity, Sita fears Ram has forgotten her, then reassures herself.
verse.sanskrit: दृश्यमाने भवेत् प्रीतिः सौहृदं नास्त्यदृश्यतः। नाशयन्ति कृतघ्नास्तु न रामो नाशयिष्यति॥
verse.line: 'Out of sight, out of mind' is true only of the ungrateful. Real love survives distance.
verse.translation: Love lasts while someone is in sight; out of sight, affection fades. But that is the way of the ungrateful. Ram will not let it fade.
verse.why: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.

matched.label: My parents are getting older far away

prasang.title: Sita in captivity
prasang.summary: Guards threaten Sita day and night. She fears Ram has forgotten her, then reminds herself that out of sight is out of mind only for the ungrateful. The guard Trijata dreams of Ram's victory, and good omens begin to appear.
prasang.story_hook: She had been alone in the grove for ten months, surrounded by guards who mocked her every day.
prasang.lesson: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.

verse.meaning: Sita sits in the ashoka grove, alone after the guards have left. She feels the weight of the distance between her and Ram, and the fear that he might have forgotten her. She speaks to herself to steady her heart, reminding herself that love fading out of sight is a trait of the ungrateful. She holds on to the truth that Ram’s love will not let her go, and that hope can come from unexpected people.
verse.for_you: The bond you share with your son is not measured by miles. It is a real thing that distance cannot break. Your heart aches because the love is still strong, and that is a good thing. Let that truth rest with you today.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing that reminds you of your son's presence.
verse.scene_line: You sit in your own ashoka grove, holding onto a love that distance cannot break.
asks: How can I tell if my love is fading or just waiting?
What if the one I love has already forgotten me?

verse.speaker: Hanuman
verse.setting: Hanuman has found Sita, terrified and alone; he works out how to speak without frightening her.
verse.sanskrit: अवश्यमेव वक्तव्यं मानुषं वाक्यमर्थवत्। मया सान्त्वयितुं शक्या नान्यथेयमनिन्दिता ॥
verse.line: To comfort someone, use their language, not the one that impresses.
verse.translation: I must speak to her in ordinary human words that carry meaning. There is no other way to comfort this blameless woman.
verse.why: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.

prasang.title: How Hanuman spoke to Sita
prasang.summary: Hanuman has found Sita but she is terrified. He thinks carefully: speak in ordinary language, not court Sanskrit; don't gamble on a fight; start by gently praising Ram so she can trust him. He sings Ram's story softly from the tree, and she hears hope for the first time: joy comes to the one who stays alive.
prasang.story_hook: He had found her at last, and now the problem was how to speak without making her scream.
prasang.lesson: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.

verse.meaning: Hanuman stands in the garden, having found Sita. She is terrified, surrounded by guards, and she does not know if he is a friend or another trick. He thinks carefully. He decides to speak in ordinary human words, not the grand court language that would frighten her more. He will use the language she knows, the words that carry meaning for her, so she can hear comfort instead of threat. He will not impress her. He will reach her.
verse.for_you: The love you carry for your son is real, but it is also a hard conversation you are having with your own mind. The waiting hurts because the bond is still alive.
verse.scene_line: You are speaking to your own fear in the only language it understands.
asks: What words would reach my son if he were here now?
How do I speak to this ache without fighting it?
What language does my heart use when it is afraid?

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.for_you: Most of what you fear hasn't happened. Your mind keeps living it in advance, again and again.

story.title: Shabari's long wait
story.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
story.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
story.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

anchor.speaker: Shabari
anchor.setting: The old ascetic woman Shabari has waited years at Pampa for Ram, as her teachers foretold.
anchor.sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महाभागैस्तदाहं पुरुषर्षभ। मया तु संचितं वन्यं विविधं पुरुषर्षभ॥ तवार्थे पुरुषव्याघ्र पम्पायास्तीरसम्भवम्।
anchor.line: I was told you would come, so I kept gathering for you. Waiting was a kind of preparing.
anchor.translation: So the great ones told me, best of men, and for you I have gathered every kind of forest food from the banks of the Pampa.
anchor.why: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

prasang.title: Shabari's long wait
prasang.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
prasang.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
prasang.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

story.hook_title: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.teaser: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.for_you: Shabari waited for years without knowing if Ram would ever come, and her waiting was not a waste. It was a way of living. Your waiting for your son is the same. It is not a flaw in your mind. It is proof that your love is real and active.
asks: Can I let the waiting be my work?
